readings.c1s1:
happy: as, an ''unfortunate'' adventure; an ''unfortunate'' man.
{{smaller block|<poem>Men ever were most blessed, till cross fate
Brought love and women forth, ''unfortunate''
To all that ever tasted of their smiles.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 4.}}}}
={{smaller|'''Syn.''' Unsuccessful, ill-fated, ill-starred, disastrous, calamitous. See ''fortunate.''}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One who or that which is unfortunate; one who has fallen into misfortune or misery.
{{smaller block|<poem>One more ''unfortunate'',
Weary of breath.</poem>
{{right|''Hood'', Bridge of Sighs.}}}}

'''unfortunately''' (un-fôr′t̮ū-nạ̄t-li), ''adv.'' In an unfortunate manner; by ill fortune; unhappily. ''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1029.

'''unfortunateness''' (un-fôr′t̮ū-nạ̄t-nes), ''n.'' The condition or state of being unfortunate; ill luck; ill fortune.
{{smaller block|His greatest ''Unfortunateness'' was in his greatest Blessing.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 102.}}}}

'''unfossiliferous''' (un-fos-i-lif′e̤-rus), ''a.'' Destitute of fossils. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XVIII. 622.

'''unfossilized''' (un-fos′il-īzd), ''a.'' Not fossilized. ''Quarterly Rev.''

'''unfostered''' (un-fos′tėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not fostered; not nourished.—'''2.''' Not countenanced or favored; not patronized: as, a scheme ''unfostered.''

'''unfought''' (un-fât′), ''a.'' Not fought.
{{smaller block|<poem>If they march along
''Unfought'' withal.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 5. 12.}}}}

'''unfounded''' (un-foun′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not founded; not built or established. ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 829.
readings.c1s2:
—'''2.''' Having no foundation; vain; idle; baseless: as, ''unfounded'' expectations. ''Paley'', Natural Theology.

'''unfoundedly''' (un-foun′ded-li), ''adv.'' In a baseless or unfounded manner.

'''unframable†''' (un-frā′ma̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being framed or molded. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, i. § 16.

'''unframableness†''' (un-frā′ma̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unframable. ''Bp. Sanderson.''

'''unframe†''' (un-frām′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''frame.''] To destroy the frame of; take apart; hence, to make useless; destroy.
{{smaller block|You write unto me that you are much offended by many slanderers that depraue your doings and ''unframe'' your attempts. ''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 109.}}

'''unframed''' (un-frāmd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not formed; not constructed; not fashioned. ''Dryden.''—'''2.''' Not provided with a frame; not put into a frame: as, an ''unframed'' picture.

'''unfranchised''' (un-fran′chizd), ''a.'' Not franchised.

'''unfrangible†''' (un-fran′ji-bl), ''a.'' Not frangible; incapable of being broken; infrangible. ''Jer. Taylor.''

'''unfrankable''' (un-frang′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being franked or sent by a public conveyance free of expense. ''Southey'', Letters (1819), iii. 106. (''Davies.'')

'''unfraught''' (un-frât′), ''a.'' Not fraught; not filled with a load or burden; unloaded.
{{smaller block|<poem>But would God that without lenger delayes
These galees were ''vnfraught'' in fortie dayes.</poem>
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 195.}}}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
'''unfree''' (un-frē′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unfre''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''free''.] Not free, in any sense of the word ''free''.
{{smaller block|Below the freeman there were ''unfree'' men, serfs bound to the soil and slaves, the conquered foes of past generations and the captives of his own.
{{right|''F. Pollock'', Land Laws, i. 16.}}
In no previous arrangement between Christian states had the rule “free ships, free goods” been separated from the opposite, “''unfree'' or hostile ships, hostile goods.”
{{right|''Woolsey'', Introd. to Inter. Law, § 174.}}}}

'''unfreeze†''' (un-frēz′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''freeze''.] To thaw.
{{smaller block|''Unfreeze'' the frost of her chaste heart.
{{right|''T. Hudson'', Judith, iv. 196. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''unfrequency''' (un-frē′kwe̤n-si), ''n.'' The state of being unfrequent; infrequency.
{{smaller block|The ''unfrequency'' of apparitions. ''Glanville'', Essays, vi.}}

'''unfrequent''' (un-frē′kwe̤nt), ''a.'' Not frequent; not common; not happening often; infrequent. ''Spectator'', No. 472.
{{smaller block|In the German universities feuds were not ''unfrequent''.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 848.}}}}

'''unfrequent†''' (un-frẹ̄-kwent′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''frequent''.] To cease to frequent. ''J. Philips'', Cider, i. [Rare.]

'''unfrequented''' (un-frẹ̄-kwen′ted), ''a.'' Not frequented; seldom resorted to by human beings; solitary: as, an ''unfrequented'' place or forest. ''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 2.

'''unfrequently''' (un-frē′kwe̤nt-li), ''adv.'' Infrequently. ''Cogan'', On the Passions, i. 2. [Rare.]
415

='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Hostile, inimical, antagonistic. See ''amicable''.}}

'''unfriendly''' (un-frend′li), ''adv.'' In an unkind manner; not as a friend. ''Wollaston'', Religion of Nature, vi.

'''unfriendship''' (un-frend′ship), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unfrindship''; < ''unfriend'' + ''-ship''.] Unfriendliness; enmity.

'''unfrighted''' (un-frī′ted), ''a.'' Not frighted; not scared or terrified. ''B. Jonson'', Epigrams, iv.

'''unfrightful''' (un-frīt′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not frightful; not terrifying or repulsive. ''Carlyle'', French Rev., I. vii. 4.

'''unfrock''' (un-frok′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''frock''.] To deprive of a frock; divest of a frock; hence, referring to a monk’s frock, to deprive of ecclesiastical rank or authority.
{{smaller block|“Proud prelate,” she [Elizabeth] wrote, . . . “If you do not immediately comply with my request, . . . I will ''unfrock'' you!”
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Short Hist. of Eng. People, vii. 3.}}}}

'''unfructed''' (un-fruk′ted), ''a.'' In ''her.'', having no fruit: said of a branch or sprig of some plant which is usually represented fructed. More leaves or sprigs are usually shown as forming part of the branch than when there is fruit.

'''unfructuous†''', ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fructuous''.] Unfruitful. ''Wyclif.''

'''unfruitful''' (un-fröt′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not fruitful, in any sense.
{{smaller block|In the midst of his ''unfruitful'' prayer.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 344.}}}}

'''unfruitfully''' (un-fröt′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In an unfruitful manner; fruitlessly. ''B. Jonson'', The Silent Woman, v. 1.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unfruitfulness''' (un-fröt′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unfruitful; barrenness; infecundity; unproductiveness: applied to persons or things.

'''unfruitous†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''unfruytous''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''fruitous'', fruitful: see ''fructuous''.] Unfruitful. ''Wyclif.''

'''unfueled, unfuelled''' (un-fū′eld), ''a.'' Not supplied with fuel; not fed with fuel. ''Southey'', Thalaba, ii. (''Davies.'') [Rare.]

'''unfulfilled''' (un-fu̇l-fild′), ''a.'' Not fulfilled; not accomplished: as, a prophecy or prediction ''unfulfilled.'' ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 511.

'''unfull†''' (un-fu̇l′), ''a.'' Not full or complete; imperfect. ''Sylvester.''

'''unfumed''' (un-fūmd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not fumigated.—'''2†.''' Not extracted or drawn forth by fumigation; undistilled: noting odor or scent.
{{smaller block|<poem>She . . . strows the ground
With rose and odours from the shrub ''unfumed.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 349.}}}}

'''unfunded''' (un-fun′ded), ''a.'' Not funded; floating: as, an ''unfunded'' debt. See ''fund''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', and ''funded.'' {{smaller|The ''unfunded debt'' of the United Kingdom exists in the form of exchequer bills and bonds, treasury bills, etc., issued by the government when it desires to raise money for temporary purposes, all bearing interest at fixed rates, and due at specified times; while the ''funded debt'' of that country is properly no debt at all, the government being under no obligation to repay the principal sum represented by the stock, but only to pay the interest}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''unfused'''<sup>1</sup> (un-fūzd′), ''a.'' Not fused; not melted.

'''unfused'''<sup>2</sup> (un-fūzd′), ''a.'' Not provided or fitted with a fuse, as a mine or a bomb. ''Science'', V. 74.

'''unfusible''' (un-fū′zi-bl), ''a.'' Infusible. [Rare.]

'''unga, ungka''' (ung′gä̤, ung′kä̤), ''n.'' The siamang.

'''ungain†''' (un-gān′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungain'', ''ungayn''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gain'', ''a.''] '''1.''' Perilous; dreadful.
{{smaller block|[He] gird gomes vnto grounde with ''vngayn'' strokes.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1332.}}}}
'''2.''' Ungainly; awkward; clumsy.
{{smaller block|A brown boy with a thin face, a huge nose, and as ''ungain'' as possible.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 86.}}}}

'''ungained''' (un-gānd′), ''a.'' Not yet gained; unpossessed. ''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 1. 315.

'''ungainful''' (un-gān′fu̇l), ''a.'' Unprofitable; not producing gain. ''Daniel'', Musophilus.

'''ungainliness''' (un-gān′li-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being ungainly; ungainly appearance; clumsiness; awkwardness.

'''ungainly''' (un-gān′li), ''a.'' [< ME. *''ungaynly'' (cf. ''ungainly'', ''adv.''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gainly'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' Unfit; vain.
{{smaller block|Misusing their knowledge to ''ungainly'' ends, as either ambition, superstition, or for satisfying their curiosity.
{{right|''Hammond'', Sermons, IV. 13.}}}}
'''2.''' Awkward; clumsy; uncouth: as, an ''ungainly'' carriage. ''Everett'', Orations, II. 213.='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|''Uncouth'', ''Bungling'', etc. See ''awkward'' and ''clumsy''.}}

'''ungainly''' (un-gān′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''ungaynly'', ''ungeinliche''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gainly'', ''adv.''] In an awkward manner; clumsily; uncouthly.
{{smaller block|Why dost thou stare and look so ''ungainly''?
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Confederacy, i. 2.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''ungallant''' (un-gal′ant, -ga-lant′), ''a.'' Not gallant; uncourtly to ladies. ''Gay'', Letter to Swift, April 27, 1731.

'''ungalled''' (un-gâld′), ''a.'' Unhurt; not galled; uninjured.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why, let the stricken deer go weep,
The hart ''ungalled'' play.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 283.}}}}

'''ungarment''' (un-gär′ment), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''garment.''] To unclothe; strip.

'''ungarmented''' (un-gär′men-ted), ''a.'' Not having garments; not covered with garments; unclothed.
{{smaller block|<poem>And round her limbs ''ungarmented'' the fire
Curl’d its fierce flakes.</poem>
{{right|''Southey'', Joan of Arc, iv. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''ungarnished''' (un-gär′nisht), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungarnyst''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''garnished.''] Not garnished or furnished; unadorned; not properly provided or equipped.
{{smaller block|The gome watz ''vngarnyst'' with god men to dele.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 137.}}}}
{{smaller block|A plain ''ungarnish’d'' present as a thanke-offering to thee.
{{right|''Milton'', Animadversions.}}}}

'''ungartered''' (un-gär′tėrd), ''a.'' Not held by garters, as the hose or stockings; not having or wearing garters.
{{smaller block|You chid at Sir Proteus for going ''ungartered.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 1. 79.}}}}

{{smaller block|Until the Lord ''unfret'' his angry brows.
{{right|''Greene and Lodge'', Looking Glass for Lond. and Eng.}}}}

'''unfretted''' (un-fret′ed), ''a.'' Not fretted; not worn or rubbed. ''Holinshed'', Chronicles of Ireland, an. 1532.

'''unfriend''' (un-frend′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unfreond'', ''onfreond'' (= MHG. ''unvriunt''), hostile person; < ''un-'' + ''friend''.] One not a friend; an enemy. ''Carlyle.''

'''unfriended''' (un-fren′ded), ''a.'' Lacking friends; not countenanced or supported. ''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 3. 10.
{{smaller block|He was ''unfriended'' and unknown.
{{right|''Ticknor'', Hist. Span. Literature, II. 97.}}}}

'''unfriendedness''' (un-fren′ded-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unfriended. ''Athenæum'', No. 3148, p. 236.

'''unfriendliness''' (un-frend′li-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being unfriendly; want of kindness; disfavor. ''Leighton'', Com. on 1 Pet. ii. 11.

'''unfriendly''' (un-frend′li), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; inimical: as, an ''unfriendly'' neighbor.
{{smaller block|<poem>I would not breed dissention;
’Tis an ''unfriendly'' office.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, ii. 3.}}
They left their bones beneath ''unfriendly'' skies.
{{right|''Cowper'', Expostulation, l. 524.}}}}
'''2.''' Not favorable; not adapted to promote or support any object.
{{smaller block|The ''unfriendly'' elements.
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iii. 1. 58.}}}} ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Hostile, inimical, antagonistic. See ''amicable''.}}

'''unfriendly''' (un-frend′li), ''adv.'' In an unkind manner; not as a friend. ''Wollaston'', Religion of Nature, vi.

'''unfriendship''' (un-frend′ship), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unfrindship''; < ''unfriend'' + ''-ship''.] Unfriendliness; enmity.

'''unfrighted''' (un-frī′ted), ''a.'' Not frighted; not scared or terrified. ''B. Jonson'', Epigrams, iv.

'''unfruitfulness''' (un-fröt′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unfruitful; barrenness; infecundity; unproductiveness: applied to persons or things.

{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 349.}}}}

'''unfunded''' (un-fun′ded), ''a.'' Not funded; floating: as, an ''unfunded'' debt. See ''fund''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', and ''funded.'' {{smaller|The ''unfunded debt'' of the United Kingdom exists in the form of exchequer bills and bonds, treasury bills, etc., issued by the government when it desires to raise money for temporary purposes, all bearing interest at fixed rates, and due at specified times; while the ''funded debt'' of that country is properly no debt at all, the government being under no obligation to repay the principal sum represented by the stock, but only to pay the interest thereon, for the due performance of which a fund consisting of the product of certain taxes or sources of revenue is set aside.}}

'''unfurl''' (un-fėrl′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''furl.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To spread or shake out from a furled state, as a sail or a flag.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gallia’s proud standards, to Bavaria’s joined,
''Unfurl'' their gilded lilies in the wind.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', The Campaign.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, to disclose; display.
{{smaller block|I am resolved to display my ''unfurled'' soule in your very face.
{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 56.}}
<poem>The red right arm of Jove,
With all his terrors there ''unfurl’d.''</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', tr. of Horace.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be spread out or expanded; open to the wind.
{{smaller block|<poem>As marks his eye the seaboy on the mast,
The anchors rise, the sails ''unfurling'' fast.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Corsair, i. 16.}}}}

'''unfurnish''' (un-fėr′nish), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''furnish.''] To deprive of furnishing, furniture, or necessaries of any kind. ''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 170.

'''unfurnished''' (un-fėr′nisht), ''a.'' Not furnished; not supplied with furnishings or furniture of any kind; unsupplied; unequipped: as, an ''unfurnished'' house.
{{smaller block|We shall be much ''unfurnish’d'' for this time.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 2. 10.}}}}

'''unfurrowed''' (un-fur′ōd), ''a.'' Not furrowed; not formed into drills or ridges; hence, smooth: as, an ''unfurrowed'' field; the ''unfurrowed'' sea.
{{smaller block|The unseeded and ''unfurrowed'' soil. ''Cowper'', Odyssey, ix.}}

'''unfused'''<sup>1</sup> (un-fūzd′), ''a.'' Not fused; not melted.

'''unfused'''<sup>2</sup> (un-fūzd′), ''a.'' Not provided or fitted with a fuse, as a mine or a bomb. ''Science'', V. 74.

'''unfusible''' (un-fū′zi-bl), ''a.'' Infusible. [Rare.]

'''unga, ungka''' (ung′gä̤, ung′kä̤), ''n.'' The siamang.

'''ungain†''' (un-gān′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungain'', ''ungayn''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gain'', ''a.''] '''1.''' Perilous; dreadful.
{{smaller block|[He] gird gomes vnto grounde with ''vngayn'' strokes.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1332.}}}}
'''2.''' Ungainly; awkward; clumsy.
{{smaller block|A brown boy with a thin face, a huge nose, and as ''ungain'' as possible.
{{right|''Gray'', Letters, I. 86.}}}}

'''ungained''' (un-gānd′), ''a.'' Not yet gained; unpossessed. ''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 1. 315.

'''ungainful''' (un-gān′fu̇l), ''a.'' Unprofitable; not producing gain. ''Daniel'', Musophilus.

'''ungainliness''' (un-gān′li-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being ungainly; ungainly appearance; clumsiness; awkwardness.

'''ungainly''' (un-gān′li), ''a.'' [< ME. *''ungaynly'' (cf. ''ungainly'', ''adv.''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gainly'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' Unfit; vain.
{{smaller block|Misusing their knowledge to ''ungainly'' ends, as either ambition, superstition, or for satisfying their curiosity.
{{right|''Hammond'', Sermons, IV. 13.}}}}
'''2.''' Awkward; clumsy; uncouth: as, an ''ungainly'' carriage. ''Everett'', Orations, II. 213.='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|''Uncouth'', ''Bungling'', etc. See ''awkward'' and ''clumsy''.}}

'''ungainly''' (un-gān′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''ungaynly'', ''ungeinliche''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''gainly'', ''adv.''] In an awkward manner; clumsily; uncouthly.
{{smaller block|Why dost thou stare and look so ''ungainly''?
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Confederacy, i. 2.}}}}

'''ungallant''' (un-gal′ant, -ga-lant′), ''a.'' Not gallant; uncourtly to ladies. ''Gay'', Letter to Swift, April 27, 1731.

'''ungalled''' (un-gâld′), ''a.'' Unhurt; not galled; uninjured.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why, let the stricken deer go weep,
The hart ''ungalled'' play.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 283.}}}}

'''ungarment''' (un-gär′ment), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''garment.''] To unclothe; strip.

'''ungarmented''' (un-gär′men-ted), ''a.'' Not having garments; not covered with garments; unclothed.
{{smaller block|<poem>And round her limbs ''ungarmented'' the fire
Curl’d its fierce flakes.</poem>
{{right|''Southey'', Joan of Arc, iv. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''ungarnished''' (un-gär′nisht), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ungarnyst''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''garnished.''] Not garnished or furnished; unadorned; not properly provided or equipped.
{{smaller block|The gome watz ''vngarnyst'' with god men to dele.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 137.}}}}
{{smaller block|A plain ''ungarnish’d'' present as a thanke-offering to thee.
{{right|''Milton'', Animadversions.}}}}

'''ungartered''' (un-gär′tėrd), ''a.'' Not held by garters, as the hose or stockings; not having or wearing garters.
{{smaller block|You chid at Sir Proteus for going ''ungartered.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 1. 79.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
